newsitem.title: USA: U.S. January trade gap soars for second month.
newsitem.headline: U.S. January trade gap soars for second month.

text.p: The U.S. trade gap soared for a second consecutive month in January, hitting its highest level in more than nine years on record imports and shrinking exports, the Commerce Department said Thursday.

The January deficit shot up 21.1 percent to $12.71 billion after a revised 31.6 percent jump in December -- the widest monthly shortfall since the fourth quarter of 1987, when deficits were running at an average $12.9 billion a month -- the department said.
The January deficit was much higher than anticipated by Wall Street economists, who had forecast a $10.7 billion shortfall.
"I think it's clearly a surprising figure," Adam Chester, an international bond analyst at Yamaichi International (London), said.
"(The figures) highlight the fact that the improvement that we saw in the trade balance in the U.S. in the fourth quarter has come to a startling halt."
"It's certainly a disappointing figure," David Sloan, an economist at I.D.E.A. Inc., said.
Both analysts said they thought the trade gap would prompt economists to lower their forecasts for the first quarter's gross domestic product.

Higher oil prices and a strong U.S. economy drew in rising imports. Meanwhile, foreign trade partners in Europe and Japan offered a less buoyant market for U.S.-made exports, fostering the back-to-back jumps in the December and January deficits.

Imports of goods and services climbed 2.2 percent to a record $83.48 billion in January, a third consecutive monthly increase. Exports fell for a second month in a row, down 0.6 percent to $70.78 billion.

The cost of imported petroleum products rose to $5.11 billion in January from $4.66 billion in December. The price per barrel of imported crude oil was up to $21.99 from $21.65, the highest since January 1991 during the Gulf War against Iraq.
As a result, the deficit with oil-producing OPEC countries climbed 41.2 percent in January to $2.66 billion.
While the politically sensitive deficit with Japan edged up 0.7 percent to $4.29 billion in January, the shortfall with China accelerated 40.8 percent to $3.72 billion.
The rising trade gap with China is likely to aggravate tensions between the two countries as the United States protests that China guards its own markets while aggressively selling overseas.
Monthly deficits with Japan may also be on a rising curve.

Japan said on Monday, in reporting its February trade numbers, that its bilateral surplus with the United States rose substantially, on a year-over-year basis, because of higher sales of cars into U.S. markets.
The United States typically runs a surplus on its trade with other countries in services, like travel and tourism, that partly offsets big merchandise trade deficits.

In January the merchandise deficit increased 12.7 percent to $19.02 billion from $16.87 billion in December. The surplus on services narrowed 1.1 percent to $6.31 billion from $6.38 billion in December.
The Commerce Department said there were record imports of industrial supplies and materials, capital goods and cars and parts during January.

Meanwhile, exports of U.S.-produced commercial aircraft plummeted by $869 million to their lowest level in a year while foreign sales of telecommunications equipment and capital goods also dropped sharply.

The bilateral deficit with Canada narrowed by 19.5 percent to $1.87 billion in January and with Western Europe it improved by 34.9 percent to $1.34 billion. But those were rare instances of improvement.
The gap with Mexico shot up 92.4 percent to $1.28 billion and the shortfall with Taiwan widened 48.2 percent to $1.07 billion in January.

Analysts said before the trade report was issued that a strong dollar, which makes U.S. exports more expensive for foreigners, together with economic weakness among key trade partners in Europe and Japan, might combine to keep the U.S. monthly deficit at lofty levels for some time.
"I would say it's a little early to talk about a big dollar impact ... but it's not too early to think about it," said Richard Koss, international economist with MFR Inc. in New York.
